questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is given a cholinergic agonist during a study of autonomic reflexes, and his heart rate slows. Activation of which of the following signaling pathways in cardiac tissue is most directly responsible for this effect?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gq-coupled receptor that increases IP3 and intracellular calcium

explanation.summary: Cardiac slowing by cholinergics is mediated by the M2 receptor, a Gi-coupled GPCR that lowers cAMP.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the heart, muscarinic M2 receptors couple to Gi, decreasing cAMP and reducing rate and AV nodal conduction. This is why parasympathetic (cholinergic) activation slows the pulse.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gq with increased IP3/Ca2+ is the M1/M3 pathway for glands and smooth muscle, not the cardiac slowing pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gs increases cAMP and would raise, not lower, heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ligand-gated Na+/K+ channels describe nicotinic (Nm) receptors at the neuromuscular junction, not cardiac muscarinic signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic receptors are GPCRs, not tyrosine kinase receptors.

questions.stem: Which muscarinic receptor subtype is primarily responsible for slowing the heart rate and impulse conduction through the cardiac nodes?

explanation.summary: The M2 receptor mediates cholinergic slowing of the heart.
explanation.whyCorrect: M2 is the dominant cardiac muscarinic receptor; via Gi it decreases cAMP and slows the pulse rate and conduction through the SA and AV nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M1 is a Gq neuronal receptor associated with cognition, memory, and learning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M3 is a Gq receptor driving gland secretion and smooth-muscle contraction, not cardiac slowing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M5 is not the clinically important cardiac subtype; M1-M3 are the key clinical receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nm is the nicotinic ligand-gated channel at skeletal muscle, unrelated to nodal slowing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man cannot void on the third postoperative day. There is no mechanical obstruction, and his bladder is markedly distended. A drug is chosen that contracts the detrusor muscle and relaxes the internal urethral sphincter to promote emptying. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Bethanechol is the direct-acting cholinergic used to treat non-obstructive urinary retention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bethanechol is an orally administered choline ester that causes bladder detrusor contraction and relaxes the urinary sphincter, treating urinary retention (and also ileus).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetylcholine is rapidly hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase and is not used therapeutically for retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atropine is an antimuscarinic; it relaxes the detrusor and would worsen retention.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Carbachol is used ophthalmically for glaucoma, not for bladder emptying.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma, not urinary retention.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome has severe dry mouth that is also worse after prior head and neck radiation. She is started on an oral agent that stimulates salivary secretion. Which of the following was most likely prescribed?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine is used orally to treat xerostomia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine, a tertiary-amine alkaloid, is used for xerostomia after head and neck radiation and in Sjogren syndrome, where disrupted lacrimal and salivary function improves with cholinergic stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic that would reduce secretions and worsen dry mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not xerostomia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is used as ophthalmic drops for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methacholine is a diagnostic bronchoprovocation agent with no other therapeutic use.

questions.stem: A patient with glaucoma is treated with cholinergic eye drops. The reduction in intraocular pressure is best explained by which of the following drug-induced effects?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxation of the bladder detrusor muscle

explanation.summary: Cholinergic drops lower intraocular pressure by contracting the pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbachol and pilocarpine cause miosis by contracting the pupillary sphincter and adjust the ciliary muscle, reducing resistance to aqueous humor outflow and thereby lowering intraocular pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics cause bronchoconstriction, not bronchodilation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cholinergics increase, not decrease, lacrimal secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis; mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bladder effects are unrelated to the ocular mechanism of pressure reduction.

questions.stem: Indirect-acting cholinomimetic agents increase parasympathetic activity through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking reuptake of norepinephrine at the synapse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Directly binding and activating muscarinic receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing synthesis of choline in the presynaptic neuron

explanation.summary: Indirect-acting cholinomimetics are cholinesterase inhibitors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike direct-acting agents that bind receptors, indirect-acting cholinomimetics inhibit acetylcholinesterase, preventing breakdown of ACh and thereby increasing PNS activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antagonizing nicotinic receptors would reduce, not increase, cholinergic transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking norepinephrine reuptake is an adrenergic action unrelated to cholinergic breakdown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That describes direct-acting cholinomimetics, not the indirect class.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing choline synthesis is not the defined mechanism of these drugs.

questions.stem: Compared with acetylcholine, choline ester drugs such as carbachol have a longer duration of action. Which of the following properties best explains this difference?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible covalent binding to the receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid renal excretion of the active drug

explanation.summary: Choline esters are longer-acting because they resist acetylcholinesterase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Modification of the choline side chain makes esters like carbachol more resistant to hydrolysis by acetylcholinesterase than ACh, giving a longer duration of action. Methacholine is the exception, being rapidly hydrolyzed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These drugs do bind and activate muscarinic receptors, which is required for their effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Their action is receptor activation, not irreversible covalent binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rapid hydrolysis would shorten, not lengthen, duration; this describes ACh (and methacholine).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Duration is explained by enzymatic resistance, not renal excretion in this brick.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with intermittent cough and suspected asthma undergoes pulmonary function testing. An inhaled agent is administered to provoke bronchoconstriction as a diagnostic challenge. Which of the following was most likely used?

explanation.summary: Methacholine is used for bronchoprovocation testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methacholine is indicated for testing bronchospastic (bronchoprovocation) activity as a diagnostic tool and, unlike the other choline esters, is rapidly hydrolyzed and has no other therapeutic use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is an antimuscarinic and would block, not provoke, bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bethanechol is used for urinary retention and ileus, not bronchial testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbachol is an ophthalmic agent for glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine is used for xerostomia and glaucoma.

questions.stem: Activation of muscarinic receptors in the gastrointestinal tract produces which of the following effects?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contraction of the internal anal sphincter

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation increases GI motility and secretions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic (M3) activation increases gastric motility and secretions and relaxes the internal anal sphincter; the increased motility can cause diarrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased motility, not decreased, is the cholinergic effect, so constipation is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The internal anal sphincter relaxes rather than contracts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastric secretions increase with cholinergic activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salivation increases with cholinergic activation.

questions.stem: Cholinergic activation of the eye produces which of the following effects?

explanation.summary: Cholinergic activation of the eye causes miosis and ciliary contraction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Muscarinic activation contracts the sphincter and ciliary muscles of the eye, producing miosis (pupil constriction) and increased lacrimation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergic activation increases lacrimation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergic drugs lower intraocular pressure, which is why they treat glaucoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis is an antimuscarinic effect, the opposite of cholinergic action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The pupillary sphincter contracts, not relaxes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with Sjogren syndrome is treated with oral pilocarpine. Which of the following adverse effects is she most likely to report, occurring in roughly half of patients?

explanation.summary: Pilocarpine commonly causes excessive sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pilocarpine is associated with excess sweating; about 50-60% of patients report this adverse effect due to cholinergic stimulation of sweat glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholinergics increase GI motility and tend toward diarrhea, not constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cholinergics increase secretions and sweating, so dry skin is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cholinergics cause miosis, not mydriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Muscarinic activation slows the heart, producing bradycardia rather than tachycardia.

questions.stem: Pilocarpine differs from choline ester cholinergics in that it is a tertiary-amine alkaloid. Which of the following properties does this structure confer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It can only be administered intravenously

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is able to cross the blood-brain barrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is rapidly degraded by acetylcholinesterase

explanation.summary: As a tertiary-amine alkaloid, pilocarpine crosses the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that pilocarpine is a tertiary amine that does cross the blood-brain barrier, distinguishing it from the choline esters.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pilocarpine is given orally and ophthalmically, not only IV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pilocarpine is a muscarinic agonist and does activate these receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Its alkaloid structure is not a substrate rapidly cleaved by acetylcholinesterase like ACh.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pilocarpine acts on muscarinic receptors, not selectively on nicotinic receptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacologist is describing how a class of drugs produces its effects. The drugs bind muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the peripheral nervous system and CNS but leave nicotinic receptors unaffected, and their actions are opposite to those of the rest-and-digest parasympathetic system. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of these drugs?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics (antimuscarinics) act by competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that anticholinergics act primarily through competitive inhibition of muscarinic receptors in the PNS, CNS, or both, and that most do not block nicotinic receptors. Their effects are therefore opposite to those of parasympathetic (cholinergic) stimulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticholinergics target muscarinic, not adrenergic, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They antagonize rather than activate muscarinic receptors; agonism would produce cholinergic (parasympathetic) effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase raises acetylcholine and produces cholinergic effects, the opposite of an anticholinergic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticholinergics generally do not block nicotinic receptors, and their muscarinic blockade is competitive and reversible.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in the emergency department has symptomatic sinus bradycardia with a heart rate of 38/min and lightheadedness. He is given intravenous atropine, and his heart rate rises to 74/min. Blockade of which receptor best explains this increase in heart rate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors on the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: M2 muscarinic receptors on the heart

choices.label: C
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle

choices.label: D
choices.text: M3 muscarinic receptors on glandular tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

explanation.summary: Atropine speeds the heart by blocking cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors, removing vagal slowing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's organ table lists the heart's effect as increased heart rate mediated by M2 receptors. Anticholinergics inhibit the parasympathetic (vagal) slowing of the heart, producing tachycardia, which is why atropine is useful in symptomatic bradycardia and AV node block.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist and does not act on beta-1 adrenergic receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Airway M3 receptors govern bronchial tone, not cardiac rate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M3 receptors on glands mediate secretions (dry mouth), not heart rate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuromuscular nicotinic receptors control skeletal muscle, not the heart rate, and are not blocked by atropine.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is planning a week-long ocean cruise and reports severe seasickness on prior trips. Her physician prescribes a transdermal patch that must be replaced after 72 hours. Which anticholinergic drug is most likely being prescribed?

explanation.summary: Scopolamine, a transdermal-patch anticholinergic, is used for motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states scopolamine (hyoscine) is usually formulated as a transdermal patch to treat motion sickness and postsurgical nausea, and that the patches are not for continuous use and should be replaced after 72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atropine is used for bradycardia, reducing secretions, and as a poisoning antidote, not as a motion-sickness patch.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats urinary urge incontinence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop used to dilate the pupil.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with COPD is prescribed an inhaled anticholinergic to add to his beta-agonist and inhaled corticosteroid. By blocking M3 receptors in the airways, this drug relieves his symptoms. Which effect on the airways is responsible for the benefit?

explanation.summary: Inhaled anticholinergics such as ipratropium cause bronchodilation and reduce mucus secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that M3 receptors in the lungs can cause bronchoconstriction; blocking them with ipratropium or tiotropium reduces mucus secretions and bronchoconstriction, lowering airway resistance and allowing easier breathing in asthma and COPD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoconstriction and increased secretions are the parasympathetic effects that anticholinergics oppose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The benefit comes from bronchodilation and decreased secretions, not increased ciliary clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surfactant production is not a described mechanism of these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes the effect to airway smooth muscle and secretions, not pulmonary vasodilation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a sudden, frequent urge to urinate with occasional involuntary leakage, and urodynamic testing shows detrusor overactivity. She is started on oxybutynin. What is the mechanism by which this drug relieves her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the bladder neck and trigone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking muscarinic receptors to slow detrusor contractions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing urine production through a renal diuretic effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxing the internal urethral sphincter to ease voiding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stimulating detrusor muscle contraction to empty the bladder

explanation.summary: Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic that slows detrusor contractions to control urge incontinence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes oxybutynin as the prototypical anticholinergic for urinary incontinence (overactive bladder); by blocking M3 receptors it slows bladder detrusor contractions, helping patients control urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oxybutynin is antimuscarinic, not an alpha-adrenergic blocker.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drug does not increase urine production; it reduces involuntary bladder contractions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics reduce detrusor overactivity; they do not work by relaxing the urethral sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating detrusor contraction would worsen urgency and leakage.

questions.stem: An ophthalmologist needs to dilate a patient's pupil to examine the retina during a funduscopic exam. Which of the following anticholinergic agents, administered as an eye drop, is most appropriate for producing mydriasis?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergic drops such as tropicamide (or atropine) dilate the pupil for eye exams.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that atropine and tropicamide drops are used to dilate the pupil for ophthalmoscopic exams; the mydriasis helps with retinal and pupillary examination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycopyrrolate does not penetrate well and is not described as an ophthalmic mydriatic agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin treats overactive bladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used as a transdermal patch for motion sickness, not as an ophthalmic dilating drop.

questions.stem: A toxicology instructor teaches the classic anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic. A poisoned patient who is described as 'mad as a hatter' is exhibiting which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased secretions, dry mouth, and thirst

explanation.summary: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to the CNS effects of anticholinergic toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick maps 'mad as a hatter' to central nervous system effects such as drowsiness, hallucinations, and coma, which result from central muscarinic blockade in agents that penetrate the CNS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dry mouth and decreased secretions correspond to 'dry as a bone'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flushed skin corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mydriasis and blurred vision correspond to 'blind as a bat'.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tachycardia (and overheating) corresponds to 'hot as a hare'.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presents with severe lower abdominal pain and states he has not urinated in several days. He has no prior urinary problems and is generally healthy but recently began an over-the-counter allergy medicine for a runny nose. Examination reveals a markedly distended bladder requiring catheterization. Which property of his allergy medication best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains diphenhydramine with anticholinergic properties

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a direct cholinergic agonist that stimulates the detrusor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a diuretic that overfilled the bladder

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that relaxes the bladder neck

explanation.summary: OTC diphenhydramine has anticholinergic properties that can cause urinary retention, especially in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case describes exactly this scenario: the allergy medicine contains diphenhydramine, an antihistamine with anticholinergic properties. By blocking muscarinic receptors it decreases detrusor contraction and causes urinary retention, a particular risk in elderly patients who also face confusion, constipation, and falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A cholinergic agonist would promote urination, not cause retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A diuretic would increase urine output; the problem was inability to void due to anticholinergic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor increases acetylcholine and cholinergic activity, opposite to what caused retention.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-blockade at the bladder neck would ease urine flow, not cause retention.

questions.stem: A patient who took a large amount of an anticholinergic agent is brought to the emergency department. On the anticholinergic toxidrome mnemonic, the finding 'dry as a bone' reflects which underlying mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone at M2 receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cutaneous vasodilation in the skin vasculature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased gut motility with delayed transit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pupillary dilation from iris sphincter blockade

explanation.summary: 'Dry as a bone' reflects inhibition of secretions, producing dry mouth, dry eyes, and decreased sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick attributes 'dry as a bone' to the general inhibition of secretions in mucous membranes and skin, giving dry mouth, dry eyes, and reduced sweating from muscarinic blockade of exocrine glands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blockade of cardiac vagal tone produces tachycardia ('hot as a hare').
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cutaneous flushing corresponds to 'red as a beet'.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased gut motility contributes to 'full as a flask' (retention/constipation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pupillary dilation corresponds to 'blind as a bat'.

questions.stem: A farm worker is brought in after exposure to an organophosphate insecticide, with copious secretions, bradycardia, and pinpoint pupils. Which anticholinergic drug is the appropriate antidote for this acetylcholine-excess (muscarinic) toxicity?

explanation.summary: Atropine is the antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, such as organophosphate or muscarine poisoning.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states atropine is an antidote for acetylcholine toxicity, including poisoning by organophosphates or muscarine-containing wild mushrooms. By competitively blocking muscarinic receptors, it reverses the excess-cholinergic secretions, bradycardia, and miosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ipratropium is an inhaled airway agent for asthma and COPD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oxybutynin is a bladder-selective agent for overactive bladder, not a poisoning antidote.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Scopolamine is used for motion sickness, not as the antidote of choice for cholinergic crisis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropicamide is an ophthalmic drop for pupil dilation.

questions.stem: A student is asked to predict adverse effects of anticholinergic drugs from their receptor actions. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of an anticholinergic agent?

explanation.summary: Anticholinergics decrease GI motility, which can lead to constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's review question confirms constipation as a correct answer: anticholinergics inhibit gut smooth muscle contraction and decrease motility, which can cause constipation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They cause tachycardia by blocking vagal tone, not bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They decrease, not increase, GI motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anticholinergics decrease secretions, causing dry mouth, not increased salivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They cause mydriasis (dilation), not miosis.

questions.stem: A neurologist notes that some antimuscarinic drugs are useful for CNS diseases while others are not, depending on how well they penetrate the brain. Which of the following best explains why ipratropium and glycopyrrolate are NOT useful in treating Parkinson disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are direct dopamine receptor antagonists in the striatum

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are rapidly metabolized in the gut wall before they are absorbed

choices.label: C
choices.text: They block nicotinic rather than muscarinic receptors in the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: They do not adequately cross into the central nervous system

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate rather than block muscarinic receptors centrally

explanation.summary: CNS penetration varies among antimuscarinics; poorly penetrating agents cannot treat central diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that muscarinic antagonists have variable CNS penetration. Certain agents (e.g., benztropine, atropine) carry greater CNS effects, whereas ipratropium and glycopyrrolate do not penetrate the CNS well and therefore are not useful in treating CNS diseases such as Parkinson disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are antimuscarinics, not dopamine antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the difference to CNS penetration, not to pre-absorption metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These drugs are muscarinic antagonists; the issue is CNS penetration, not a switch to nicotinic blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They block, rather than stimulate, muscarinic receptors.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis takes an over-the-counter H1 antihistamine and notices that her runny nose improves. This symptom relief is most directly explained by which of the following actions of the drug on endothelial cells adjacent to vascular smooth muscle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct stimulation of mast cell degranulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of nitric oxide and prostacyclin release

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines reduce nasal symptoms by blocking H1 receptors, which inhibits nitric oxide and prostacyclin release and produces vasoconstriction.
explanation.whyCorrect: By antagonizing H1 receptors on endothelial cells, the drug inhibits the release of nitric oxide and prostacyclin. This causes vasoconstriction and reduces edema formation, lessening runny nose symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H1 antihistamines act on histamine receptors, not nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking gastric acid secretion is a function of H2 blockers, not H1 antihistamines used for allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor; they do not trigger mast cell degranulation, which is what releases histamine in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased nitric oxide and prostacyclin would cause vasodilation and worsen edema, the opposite of the drug's effect.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man takes diphenhydramine for allergies and becomes very drowsy, while his coworker taking loratadine for the same allergies reports no sedation. Which property of diphenhydramine best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is hydrophilic and cannot enter the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: It selectively blocks H2 receptors in the stomach

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine are lipophilic and cross the blood-brain barrier, blocking central H1 receptors and causing sedation.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, so they block central H1 receptors that normally promote wakefulness, producing drowsiness. Second-generation drugs like loratadine are hydrophilic and penetrate the brain poorly, so they are non-sedating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation, not a second-generation, antihistamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that is precisely why it enters the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Diphenhydramine blocks H1, not H2 receptors, and H2 blockade would not explain sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug blocks H1 receptors; it does not stimulate central histamine release.

questions.stem: A patient is prescribed a non-sedating antihistamine for chronic urticaria so that daytime alertness is preserved. Which of the following agents best fits this description?

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines such as fexofenadine are non-sedating because they poorly cross the blood-brain barrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fexofenadine is a second-generation H1 antihistamine. These agents are hydrophilic, act primarily on peripheral H1 receptors, and cause little sedation, making them ideal when alertness must be preserved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorpheniramine is a first-generation agent that crosses the blood-brain barrier and can cause sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diphenhydramine is a lipophilic first-generation agent that causes marked drowsiness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine and is sedating.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is a first-generation agent with sedating and antimuscarinic properties.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man is brought in for confusion, blurred vision, dry mouth, and difficulty urinating that began after he started an over-the-counter first-generation antihistamine. These findings are best explained by the drug's action at which of the following receptors?

explanation.summary: Many first-generation antihistamines also block muscarinic receptors, producing anticholinergic side effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-generation H1 antihistamines have antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) activity. Blockade of muscarinic receptors causes dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, and, especially in the elderly, confusion and delirium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2 blockade relates to bronchial and vascular tone, not dry mouth and urinary retention.
whyWrongByChoice.B: D2 blockade causes extrapyramidal effects, not the dry mouth, blurred vision, and urinary retention seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H2 receptors regulate gastric acid; blocking them does not cause this anticholinergic toxidrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nicotinic receptor blockade would affect the neuromuscular junction and autonomic ganglia, not this pattern of anticholinergic findings.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant has persistent nausea and vomiting. Her physician prescribes doxylamine in combination with which of the following, an FDA-approved regimen for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy?

explanation.summary: Doxylamine plus vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is an approved treatment for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that doxylamine, a first-generation antihistamine, combined with vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), is approved for the treatment of nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. First-generation agents cross the placenta but are unlikely to be strong risk factors for major birth defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects but is not the antiemetic partner of doxylamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 is used for pernicious anemia, not paired with doxylamine for pregnancy nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin C is not part of this regimen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin D addresses bone and calcium metabolism, not nausea of pregnancy.

questions.stem: A family planning a road trip asks for a medication to prevent motion sickness in an adult. Which antihistamine is most appropriate, and what property makes it effective for this indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cetirizine, because it is hydrophilic and non-sedating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desloratadine, because it blocks H2 receptors in the brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fexofenadine, because it acts only at peripheral sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loratadine, because it is non-sedating and long acting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promethazine, because of its antimuscarinic properties

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines with antimuscarinic activity, such as promethazine, are effective against motion sickness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that first-generation antihistamines like promethazine and dimenhydrinate have antimuscarinic properties that make them effective in treating motion sickness. Second-generation agents lack this activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cetirizine is a second-generation agent lacking meaningful antimuscarinic effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Desloratadine is an H1, not H2, agent and is second-generation; it is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fexofenadine acts only peripherally and is not used for motion sickness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loratadine is a peripherally acting second-generation agent without the antimuscarinic activity needed for motion sickness.

questions.stem: In a review of histamine physiology, a student notes where the H1 receptor is located relative to other histamine receptor subtypes. According to the brick, where are H2 histamine receptors primarily located?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems

explanation.summary: H2 histamine receptors are found primarily in gastric cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that H2 histamine receptors are primarily in gastric cells, H3 receptors in the neurons, and H4 receptors in the bone marrow, whereas H1 receptors are widespread and are the target of antihistamine therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bone marrow is the location of H4, not H2, receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The neurons are where H3 receptors are located.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vascular endothelial cells express the H1 receptors targeted by antihistamines, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widespread distribution in the central and peripheral nervous systems describes H1 receptors.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old child is given a first-generation antihistamine and, instead of becoming sleepy, develops restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia. This response is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sign of H2 receptor blockade

choices.label: C
choices.text: A withdrawal effect from stopping the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: An allergic reaction to the drug

explanation.summary: First-generation antihistamines can cause paradoxical CNS stimulation in children younger than about six years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick warns that in children younger than six, first-generation antihistamines can, at regular doses, cause a paradoxical CNS stimulation manifesting as restlessness, nervousness, and insomnia rather than the usual drowsiness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: These first-generation agents act at H1 and muscarinic receptors, not H2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The reaction occurred after taking the drug, not after stopping it, so it is not withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The symptoms are a CNS drug effect, not an allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The child is stimulated, not sedated, so this is not the expected sedative effect.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman takes diphenhydramine for seasonal allergies. Through its anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) action, this drug is most likely to produce which of the following effects in the eye?

explanation.summary: Antimuscarinic action at the eye causes pupil dilation and reduced tear formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 2 lists the ocular anticholinergic effects as mydriasis (dilation) and decreased lacrimation, which clinically produce blurred vision and dry eyes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimuscarinic effects decrease, not increase, intestinal motility, causing constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antimuscarinic activity decreases sweating rather than increasing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antimuscarinic activity decreases urination, causing retention, not increased output.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Miosis and increased tears are cholinergic effects, the opposite of antimuscarinic blockade.

questions.stem: A patient taking a second-generation antihistamine for allergies reports only a mild headache and occasional fatigue, with no significant dry mouth or drowsiness. This favorable side-effect profile compared with first-generation agents is best explained by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced release of histamine from mast cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Greater lipophilicity and stronger blood-brain barrier penetration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible binding to H1 receptors in the brain

explanation.summary: Second-generation antihistamines penetrate the brain poorly and have little antimuscarinic activity, so side effects are mild and non-specific.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because second-generation agents are hydrophilic and act mainly on peripheral H1 receptors, they cause much less sedation and few antimuscarinic effects. Their adverse effects are usually mild and non-specific, such as headache, diarrhea, or fatigue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines block the H1 receptor and do not enhance histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Greater lipophilicity and brain penetration would increase, not decrease, sedation, and describes first-generation agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H1 antihistamines are competitive (reversible) H1 blockers, not irreversible binders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These drugs block H1 receptors; nicotinic blockade is not their mechanism.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man reports several weeks of new daytime sleepiness. Medication review reveals he recently added an over-the-counter pill containing diphenhydramine to help him sleep. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to address his sleepiness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a second-generation antihistamine on top of the diphenhydramine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an H2 blocker to counteract the sedation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to promethazine for its antimuscarinic effect

explanation.summary: Sedation from a first-generation antihistamine is managed by stopping the offending drug and substituting a non-sedating agent if needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the case, the patient's new sleepiness is caused by diphenhydramine, a sedating first-generation antihistamine. The remedy is to stop that drug and, if antihistamine therapy is still needed, replace it with a non-sedating second-generation agent such as loratadine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adding another antihistamine keeps the sedating diphenhydramine on board and does not fix the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An H2 blocker treats gastric acid and would not counteract the sedation from an H1 agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing the dose of the sedating drug would worsen the sleepiness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Promethazine is another sedating first-generation agent and would not relieve the drowsiness.

questions.stem: H1 antihistamines are best classified pharmacologically as which of the following with respect to the H1 receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competitive antagonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full agonists at the H1 receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective agonists at H2 and H3 receptors

explanation.summary: H1 antihistamines act by competitively binding to H1 receptors as antagonists or inverse agonists.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes H1 antihistamines as histamine antagonists and inverse agonists that work by competitively binding to H1 receptors, thereby blocking histamine's effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: They are receptor blockers, not enzymes that degrade histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They oppose, rather than activate, the H1 receptor, so they are not full agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They block the receptor; they do not inhibit histamine synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They target the H1 receptor and are not agonists at H2 or H3 receptors.
